Chapter 6: Cultivating a Superforecaster’s Mindset.
So, now that we've explored the power of habits and the importance of group dynamics, what’s the next step? Well, it’s all about developing the kind of mindset that makes accurate forecasting possible.
And here’s the good news: this isn’t some rare talent you’re born with. It’s really about adopting certain attitudes and approaches—things anyone can learn with a bit of intention and practice.
At the heart of a superforecaster’s mindset, you’ll find two qualities: intellectual humility and a relentless sense of curiosity. Instead of just looking for reasons to prove themselves right, superforecasters are always searching for evidence that might prove them wrong. Every prediction? It’s treated like a hypothesis to test—not a belief to defend at all costs.
Think of it like this: imagine a gardener tending to a patch of earth. They don’t assume every single seed will grow, or that every plant will flourish. Instead, they keep a close eye on things, ready to adapt—maybe pulling a weed here, trying a new method there. That’s exactly how superforecasters approach their own thinking. They’re always on the lookout for mental weeds—those pesky biases—and they nurture the habits that help their insights grow.
So, how do you actually start building this mindset? Here are a few techniques that really work:
First, make it a habit to actively seek contradiction. Ask yourself, “What kind of evidence would make me rethink my position?” Look for information that challenges your assumptions instead of confirming them.
Next, embrace uncertainty. Get comfortable with saying things like, “I’m not totally sure, but this is my best estimate.” Don’t feel pressured to sound more confident than the facts allow.
Another powerful tool is perspective-taking. Try putting yourself in someone else’s shoes. How might a person with a completely different background, or different experiences, see this same problem?
And finally, make time to reflect on your past predictions. Look back: where were you a little too confident? Where did you overlook uncertainty? This honest review is how you get better.
Here’s a quick real-world example. Imagine you’re weighing whether a new policy will work. Instead of just looking for reasons it might succeed—especially if you’re rooting for it—a superforecaster would go out of their way to find examples where similar policies actually failed. That willingness to challenge your own thinking? That’s what sets a great forecaster apart.
Over time, these habits start to feel natural. You begin to care more about being less wrong than being right, and you start to see every prediction as a chance to learn something new. And the best part? This mindset is just as useful for navigating life’s uncertainties as it is for making forecasts.
